title: Utility-First CSS With Tailwind 4
summary: Style with utility classes in Tailwind CSS 4.3: setup with Vite, variants, responsive design, themes as CSS variables, and markup that stays readable.
intro: Tailwind is how most new React and Next.js projects style their pages, the React course uses it from the first component, and job listings ask for it by name. A Tailwind page looks strange at first: elements with ten or fifteen short class names each, and hardly any CSS file in sight. Once you know the idea behind it and how its names are built, those lists read as plainly as a stylesheet. This lesson teaches Tailwind CSS 4.3: what utility-first means and how Tailwind writes only the CSS you use, how to set it up with Vite, its scales and its variants for hover, focus, and other states, responsive design and dark mode, your own theme as CSS variables, and the habits that keep a Tailwind project readable as it grows.

steps.title: Utility-first CSS

examples.title: Running Tailwind by hand
examples.prompt: In a folder with `tailwindcss` and `@tailwindcss/cli` installed, the frameworks lesson's button saved as `index.html`, and a file `src/input.css` holding one line, `@import "tailwindcss";`, run Tailwind's command-line tool.
examples.explanation: `-i` names the input, your CSS, and `-o` the output file to write. Tailwind scanned the folder, found `index.html`, and wrote `dist/output.css` in 23 milliseconds. The file came to about 6 kB: the rules for the button's ten classes, the theme variables those rules use, and Preflight, Tailwind's reset, which the next part explains. Add a class to `index.html`, run it again, and its rule appears. Delete the button, and its rules disappear. `--watch` keeps the tool running and writes the file again on every save, and `--minify` writes it without spaces, but with Vite you'll rarely need either.

steps.title: Setting up Tailwind 4
steps.body:
In a real project you want Tailwind to run by itself, inside the build you already have. With Vite, that's two packages, one line in the config, and one line of CSS.

## Installing

Tailwind comes in two packages: `tailwindcss` itself, and `@tailwindcss/vite`, a **plugin** for Vite, a package that adds a step to Vite's work. Both are build tools, so they're dev dependencies. In the notes project from the bundling lesson:

```bash
npm install -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite
```

npm prints how many packages it added, as it did for Vite. Then add the plugin to `vite.config.js` (example 1).

## One line of CSS

In the stylesheet that `main.js` imports, `src/style.css`, replace everything with:

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
```

That's the whole setup, and the build in example 2 shows it working. Version 3, which you'll still find in older projects, needed a `tailwind.config.js` file, three `@tailwind` lines, and a list of files to scan. Version 4, from 2025, moved its settings into your CSS, as later parts show, and finds the files to scan by itself. If you see a `tailwind.config.js` in a project, it's version 3, or version 4 still reading an old config through an `@config` line.

## Which files it scans

Tailwind scans every file in the project folder, except:

- files listed in `.gitignore`, the file that tells git what to ignore, which usually keeps out `dist`,
- anything in `node_modules`,
- CSS files, lockfiles, and binary files, like images.

When classes live somewhere it skips, like a package of your company's components in `node_modules`, add an `@source` line with a path relative to the CSS file, like `@source "../node_modules/@acme/ui";`. To leave a folder out, use `@source not "../src/legacy";`.

## Preflight

`@import "tailwindcss"` also brings **Preflight**, Tailwind's reset, the same idea as Bootstrap's Reboot, but stricter:

- Every margin is removed, so paragraphs and headings sit right against each other.
- Headings are the same size and weight as plain text, and lists lose their bullets.
- Every element gets `border: 0 solid`, so a `border` class only has to add a width.
- Images and videos become blocks that never grow wider than their container.

The surprise for newcomers is the headings: an `<h1>` looks like a paragraph until you style it. That's on purpose. Every heading's size becomes a choice you make, and its tag is left free to say what it means, for screen readers and search engines.

## Layers

Tailwind puts all the CSS it writes in the cascade layers from the cascade lesson, `theme`, `base`, `components`, and `utilities`, in that order. Preflight goes in `base` and the classes in `utilities`, so a class always beats a base style. Your own CSS outside any layer beats all of them, which matters when you mix the two, as part 5 shows.

## Browsers

Tailwind 4 uses recent CSS, like cascade layers, `@property`, and `oklch()` colors, so it needs Safari 16.4, Chrome 111, Firefox 128, or newer. That covers every current browser, and a site that must work in older ones stays on version 3.

examples.title: Adding the Vite plugin
examples.prompt: `vite.config.js` in the notes project, with Tailwind's plugin added.
examples.explanation: `plugins` is a list of functions that add steps to Vite's work, and `tailwindcss()` makes Tailwind's. From now on, whenever Vite meets a CSS file that imports Tailwind, the plugin scans the project and writes the CSS, both in the dev server and in the build. In the dev server, adding a class to a file and saving it adds the rule and swaps the stylesheet in with HMR, from the bundling lesson, so the page updates without a reload. If the project already had a `server` setting, like the port and proxy from the bundling lesson, it stays next to `plugins` in the same object.

steps.title: Utilities, variants, and states
steps.body:
Tailwind has thousands of classes, but they're built from a few patterns. Learn the patterns, and you can guess most names before you look them up.

```diagram tailwind-css-class-anatomy
A class name read left to right: when it applies, then what it sets.
```

The diagram takes one class apart. Everything before a colon is a condition, and the rest names a property and a value. So `md:hover:bg-blue-700` sets the background to `blue-700`, but only from medium screens up, and only on hover.

## The scales

**Spacing.** Padding, margin, gap, width, and height share one scale, built on a single variable, `--spacing`, which is 0.25rem. The number in a class multiplies it: `p-1` is 0.25rem, `p-4` is 1rem, and `p-8` is 2rem, and any whole number works. `px-` and `py-` set two sides, `pt-` one side, and `-mt-2` is a negative margin. `w-full` is 100%, and fractions like `w-1/2` work too.

**Color.** The palette has families, like `slate`, `gray`, `red`, `amber`, `green`, `blue`, and `violet`, each with shades from 50, almost white, to 950, almost black. `bg-blue-600`, `text-gray-700`, `border-red-500`, and `outline-amber-400` all use the same palette, and a slash sets the opacity: `bg-blue-600/50` is that blue at half strength. There's also `white`, `black`, `transparent`, and `current`, the element's text color.

**Type.** `text-xs` to `text-9xl` set the size, each with a line height that suits it. `font-medium` and `font-bold` set the weight, and `leading-tight` and `tracking-wide` the line height and letter spacing on their own.

**Layout.** `flex`, `grid`, `items-center`, `justify-between`, `gap-4`, and `grid-cols-3` are the Flexbox and Grid properties from the layout lesson, almost word for word.

## Variants

A **variant** is a prefix and a colon that makes a class apply only under some condition. Each one becomes the selector or media query you'd have written by hand, as example 2 shows.

- **States:** `hover:`, `focus:`, `focus-visible:`, `active:`, `disabled:`, `checked:`, `user-invalid:`, and `placeholder:` are the pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements from the selectors lesson. `hover:` only applies on devices that can hover, so a tap on a phone doesn't leave a button stuck in its hover color.
- **ARIA and data:** `aria-expanded:` applies when `aria-expanded="true"`, and `data-active:` when the element has a `data-active` attribute. They style an element by its real state, the same attribute a screen reader reads, so the looks and the meaning can't drift apart.
- **Groups:** mark a parent with `group`, and `group-hover:underline` on a child underlines it whenever the pointer is anywhere over the parent, so a whole card can react as one.
- **Peers:** mark an element with `peer`, and `peer-user-invalid:block` on a later sibling shows that sibling when the peer is invalid, like an error message under a field. It has to come after the peer in the HTML, because CSS can only select later siblings.

Variants stack, as in the diagram: `dark:hover:bg-gray-800` applies in dark mode, on hover.

## Arbitrary values

When the scale doesn't have what you need, square brackets take any value: `top-[117px]`, `bg-[#bada55]`, or `grid-cols-[200px_1fr]`, with an underscore standing in for a space. A custom property of your own goes in parentheses: `bg-(--brand-color)`. Use them sparingly. Every arbitrary value steps off the scale that keeps a design consistent, and needing a lot of them usually means the theme is missing a value, which part 5 shows how to add.

examples.title: A card and a field that react
examples.prompt: A trail card that reacts as one on hover, an email field whose error shows only after someone has typed a wrong value, and a menu button styled by its ARIA state.
examples.code:
Lake Loop

A gentle 5 km loop.

Enter an email address.
examples.explanation: The link is marked `group`, so hovering anywhere on the card turns its border blue and, through `group-hover:`, its title too. `focus-visible:` draws an outline only for keyboard focus. The input is marked `peer`, and the message after it starts `hidden` and becomes a block through `peer-user-invalid:block`. `:user-invalid`, from the forms lesson, only matches after someone has changed the field, so the error doesn't greet a visitor before they've typed a thing. The menu button turns gray when a script sets `aria-expanded="true"`, the same attribute a screen reader announces, so the look and the meaning stay together.

examples.title: What those variants became
examples.prompt: Part of the stylesheet Tailwind wrote for example 1: the rules for its variants, copied from `dist/output.css`.
examples.explanation: `hover:` became `:hover` inside `@media (hover: hover)`, the media feature for devices that can hover. `group-hover:` became a selector that matches the child when any `.group` above it is hovered, and `peer-user-invalid:` uses `~`, the combinator for a later sibling, which is why the peer must come first. `:where()` adds nothing to the specificity, so these rules weigh the same as a plain class. `aria-expanded:` is an attribute selector, and `disabled:` the `:disabled` pseudo-class. Every one is CSS you could have written yourself, and reading the output like this is the quickest way to find out why a class isn't doing what you expected.

steps.title: Responsive design and dark mode
steps.body:
Every page has to work on a phone, a laptop, and everything between, in a light theme and a dark one. Tailwind handles both with variants too, which keeps each size and theme of an element on the element itself.

## Breakpoints are min-width

Tailwind's breakpoints are variants: `sm:` from 40rem (640 pixels), `md:` from 48rem (768), `lg:` from 64rem (1,024), `xl:` from 80rem (1,280), and `2xl:` from 96rem (1,536). Like Bootstrap's, they're mobile first. A class without a prefix applies at every width, and `md:` applies from that width up. So you style for the phone first, then add what changes on bigger screens, like `grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3` (example 1).

The common mistake is reading `sm:` as on small screens. It means from the small breakpoint up, so `sm:text-center` centers text on everything except the smallest screens. To style only below a breakpoint, use the `max-` variants: `max-sm:hidden` hides something below 40rem. They combine into ranges, so `md:max-xl:flex` applies from `md` up to just below `xl`.

## Container queries

Recall container queries from the CSS lessons: a component that adapts to the space it's given, not the window. Tailwind has them built in. Mark the parent with `@container`, and use `@sm:`, `@md:`, `@lg:`, and the rest on the elements inside it: `@md:flex-row` applies when the container is at least 28rem wide. The same card can then lay itself out in a row in a wide column and stack in a narrow sidebar, with no change to its classes. There's `@max-md:` too, and a name, like `@container/card` with `@md/card:`, picks which container to measure when they're nested.

## Dark mode

`dark:` applies a class in dark mode, as in `bg-white dark:bg-gray-950`. By default, dark mode means the visitor's system setting, through the `prefers-color-scheme` media feature from the CSS lessons.

Many sites also offer a switch, so dark mode has to follow an attribute you set, not only the system. Redefine the variant in your CSS with `@custom-variant`, right after the import:

```css
@import "tailwindcss";

@custom-variant dark (&:where([data-theme="dark"], [data-theme="dark"] *));
```

The `&` stands for the element with the class, and the rest says: when it, or anything above it, has `data-theme="dark"`. Now `dark:` follows that attribute, and a small script sets it on `<html>` from the visitor's choice or the system setting, like the one in the Bootstrap lesson with `data-theme` in place of `data-bs-theme`. Example 2 shows the CSS that came out.

examples.title: A trail grid and a card that fits its slot
examples.prompt: A list of trail cards: one column on phones, two from `md`, three from `lg`. Each card is its own container, so it lays itself out by its own width.
examples.code:
• Lake Loop

    A gentle 5 km loop around the lake.
examples.explanation: The list is a grid with one column, then two from 48rem, then three from 64rem, all from one set of classes. Each list item is a container, so the article inside asks how wide its card is, not the window: when a card is at least 28rem wide, the photo and the text sit side by side, and in a narrower card they stack. That happens in the one-column phone layout, where cards are wide, and in a three-column layout on a big screen, where they're narrow. The description is hidden below 40rem with `max-sm:hidden`, to keep phone cards short. The two `dark:` classes darken the border and soften the text in dark mode.

examples.title: The CSS behind breakpoints and dark mode
examples.prompt: The end of the utilities layer Tailwind wrote for example 1, with the `@custom-variant` line from the body in the CSS file.
examples.explanation: Each breakpoint became a media query with the range syntax from the CSS lessons: `width >= 48rem` for `md:`, and `width < 40rem` for `max-sm:`. Tailwind writes the queries in order of width, so a larger breakpoint always comes later and wins over a smaller one, which is what makes mobile first work. The `@md:` classes became one `@container` query, measured on the nearest element with `container-type: inline-size`, which is what `@container` sets. The `dark:` classes now use the `@custom-variant` selector, with `:where()` around the attribute part, so a `dark:` class weighs the same as any other class and doesn't win just because its selector is longer.

steps.title: Your theme with @theme
steps.body:
Every site has its own brand colors, fonts, and sizes, and writing them as arbitrary values everywhere would make a mess. In Tailwind 4, they go in your CSS, in a `@theme` block, and every value you put there becomes both a CSS variable and a set of classes.

## Tokens become variables and classes

Inside `@theme`, each custom property's name says what kind of value it is, and that decides which classes it makes (example 1):

| Name | Example | Makes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--color-*` | `--color-brand-600` | `bg-brand-600`, `text-brand-600`, and every other color class |
| `--font-*` | `--font-display` | `font-display` |
| `--text-*` | `--text-huge` | `text-huge` |
| `--radius-*` | `--radius-card` | `rounded-card` |
| `--shadow-*` | `--shadow-soft` | `shadow-soft` |
| `--breakpoint-*` | `--breakpoint-3xl` | the `3xl:` variant |
| `--spacing` | `--spacing: 0.25rem` | the whole spacing scale |

Tailwind's own defaults are defined the same way, so `--color-blue-600` and `--breakpoint-md` are theme variables it ships with. Set one again to change it, like `--font-sans` for the default font. To remove a whole group, like every default color so the team can only use the brand's, set it to `initial`: `--color-*: initial;`.

## They're real CSS variables

In the stylesheet Tailwind writes, every theme variable in use appears on `:root`, in the `theme` layer, and the classes read it with `var()` (example 2). So your own CSS can use the same tokens, as in `color: var(--color-brand-600)`, and JavaScript can read them with `getComputedStyle`. Change a value in `@theme`, and every class and rule that uses it follows.

Tailwind's palette is written in `oklch()`, the color format from the CSS lessons whose lightness numbers match what eyes see, so `blue-600` and `green-600` look about equally dark. Write your own colors in `oklch()` too, with similar lightness steps, and your shades will sit well next to Tailwind's.

## Your own utilities and variants

`@utility` defines a new class that works like Tailwind's own, variants and all. After `@utility content-auto { content-visibility: auto; }`, both `content-auto` and `lg:content-auto` work. `@custom-variant`, from the last part, defines a new variant.

`@variant` goes the other way: it uses a variant inside a rule you wrote by hand, so the rule follows Tailwind's dark mode, or a breakpoint, along with everything else. Example 1 uses it, and in example 2 it became a media query.

## Layers and your own CSS

Recall the cascade lesson: CSS outside any layer beats every layer, whatever the specificity. Tailwind's classes live in the `utilities` layer, so a plain `.card { padding: 2rem; }` in your stylesheet beats `p-4` on the same element, and the class seems to do nothing. Put your own component styles in `@layer components`, which comes before `utilities`, and a class on the element wins again, the way you'd expect. Example 1 does that too.

examples.title: A theme for the trail site
examples.prompt: `src/style.css` with the site's colors, a display font, a corner radius, and an extra breakpoint, plus one utility and one component of its own.
examples.explanation: The `@theme` block adds three brand greens, written in `oklch()` with the same hue, 160, and falling lightness, a display font, a corner radius, and a breakpoint at 120rem for very wide screens. From these, Tailwind makes `bg-brand-600`, `text-brand-50`, `font-display`, `rounded-card`, a `3xl:` variant, and the rest. `@utility` adds `content-auto`, which tells the browser it may skip drawing a section until it's near the screen. `.trail-note` is a component of the site's own, in the `components` layer so classes can still change it, and it uses the theme's variables, with `@variant dark` for its dark background. The page uses them as `class="content-auto rounded-card bg-brand-600 p-6 text-white 3xl:p-10"`.

examples.title: What the theme turned into
examples.prompt: The three layers Tailwind wrote for example 1, with the page from its explanation, copied from the output.
examples.explanation: The theme layer holds real custom properties on `:root`, and only the ones something uses: the three greens, the display font, and the radius, next to Tailwind's own, like `--spacing` and the default fonts Preflight needs. The new breakpoint isn't there, since it's only needed inside the media query at the end. Each class reads its variable with `var()`, so changing a value in `@theme` changes every class that uses it. `@variant dark` became `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, because this file uses the default dark mode, without the `@custom-variant` line. The odd `.\33 xl` is how CSS writes a class name that starts with a digit, `3xl:p-10`, and you'll never type it yourself.

steps.title: Keeping Tailwind maintainable
steps.body:
Tailwind is easy to start with and easy to make a mess of. A few habits, the ones teams settle on after their first big project, keep class lists readable and the styles predictable.

## Extract components, not CSS

When the same class list appears on every button, the fix is a component: write the button once, in one place, and use it everywhere. In React, that's a `Button` component, as the React course shows. On a plain site, it's a template or a JavaScript function that makes the element. The list lives in one file, and changing every button means changing one line.

Tailwind also has `@apply`, which copies classes into a rule of your own, as in `.btn { @apply rounded-lg px-4 py-2 font-semibold; }`. It's useful for HTML you can't add classes to, like a library's markup, or articles turned into HTML from Markdown, a plain-text way of writing headings, lists, and links. Used everywhere, though, it brings back everything utility-first was meant to avoid: invented names, styles in another file, and CSS nobody dares delete.

## clsx and tailwind-merge

Components need to change their classes: a button that's sometimes disabled, a link that's sometimes active. Gluing strings together with `+` and `?` gets unreadable fast, and two small packages from npm take care of it (example 2):

- **clsx** joins class names and skips any that are false, `null`, or `undefined`, so `clsx("px-4", isActive && "bg-blue-600")` gives `"px-4 bg-blue-600"` when it's active, and `"px-4"` when it isn't.
- **tailwind-merge** solves a subtler problem. When an element has two classes that set the same property, like `px-4` and `px-2`, the winner is whichever one Tailwind wrote later in the stylesheet, not whichever comes later in `class`. So a component that accepts extra classes from outside can't reliably change its own. `twMerge` drops the losing class, keeping the last of each kind, so the extra class always wins.

Teams usually wrap the two in one small function, by habit called `cn`.

## Class order

Long class lists are easier to read when every file orders them the same way: layout first, then spacing, sizes, type, color, and states last. Nobody sorts them by hand. `prettier-plugin-tailwindcss`, a plugin for Prettier, a tool that formats code the same way every time, sorts them every time you save, in the same order Tailwind writes its CSS.

## Write class names out in full

The scanner reads your files as text, as part 1 showed, and never runs your code. A class name that only exists once your code runs, like the one this function builds, is never in any file:

```javascript
export function statusClass(status) {
  return `bg-${status === "done" ? "green" : "red"}-600`;
}
```

Its CSS is never written, so the element silently gets no color (example 1). Write every class name out in full, for instance in an object that maps each status to its classes. When a class truly can't appear in any file, like a color someone picks in a content management system, an app where people write a site's pages without touching code, `@source inline("bg-red-600 bg-green-600")` in your CSS adds those classes by name.

## When Tailwind fits

Tailwind fits best when pages are built from components, as in React, Vue, and Svelte apps, and for teams that want one design scale everyone sticks to. It fits less well when the HTML comes from somewhere you don't control, like articles written in a content management system, where the official `@tailwindcss/typography` plugin and its `prose` class help, and on teams that prefer their CSS in stylesheets. Either way, it's CSS underneath, and everything from the CSS lessons still applies. Tailwind is only a faster way to write it.

That's the end of this course. You can build a page from HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, ship it fast, and read the frameworks teams put on top. The React course starts from here.

examples.title: The class that was never written
examples.prompt: `src/badge.js` holds `statusClass` from the body, and a fixed version that looks up full class names: `done` maps to `"bg-green-700 text-white"`, and `late` to `"bg-amber-600 text-black"`. Build, then list every background class in the output.
examples.explanation: `grep` lists every background class in the stylesheet, and only two are there: the ones from the fixed version, written out in full. `bg-green-600` and `bg-red-600` are missing, because no file ever contains those words. The scanner saw `bg-`, `green`, `red`, and `-600` as separate scraps, and none of them is a class. Nothing warns you about this: the build succeeds, and the badge just has no background. When a class seems to do nothing, search the built CSS for it, as here. If it isn't there, the scanner never saw it whole.

examples.title: Joining and merging classes
examples.prompt: `classes.mjs`, run with `node classes.mjs` in a project after `npm install clsx tailwind-merge`. `cn` is the helper most teams write.
examples.output:
rounded-lg px-4 py-2 font-semibold bg-blue-600 text-white
rounded-lg px-4 py-2 font-semibold px-2
rounded-lg py-2 font-semibold px-2
rounded-lg px-4 py-2 font-semibold hover:bg-blue-700 bg-green-600
examples.explanation: `clsx` kept the active classes and dropped `opacity-50`, since `isDisabled && ...` is `false`. The second line glues `px-2` on by hand, and both `px-4` and `px-2` stay. On the page, `px-4` would win, because Tailwind writes `.px-4` after `.px-2` in the stylesheet, so the override does nothing. `twMerge` sees that the two set the same thing and drops `px-4`, keeping the last one. `cn` does both. The `...` in `...inputs` gathers every argument it's given into one array, which it passes to `clsx` to join, and then `twMerge` drops `bg-blue-600` in favor of the later `bg-green-600`, and keeps `hover:bg-blue-700`, since a hover class doesn't conflict with a plain one.

recap:
- Utility-first means styling with one-job classes in the HTML, and Tailwind writes CSS only for the classes it finds.
- With Vite, install tailwindcss and @tailwindcss/vite, add the plugin, and write @import "tailwindcss" in your CSS.
- Preflight removes default margins and heading sizes, and Tailwind's CSS lives in the theme, base, components, and utilities layers.
- Class names read left to right: variants like md:, hover:, and dark:, then a property and a value from a scale.
- Breakpoint variants are min-width, max- variants go below, and @container with @md: sizes a component by its slot.
- @theme turns tokens into CSS variables and classes, and @utility, @variant, and @custom-variant extend Tailwind.
- Repeat a class list through a component, merge classes with clsx and tailwind-merge, and never build class names at runtime.
